extracted.intended_audience: judges, juries, and patent litigators in U.S. federal patent trials (AIPLA model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials explaining claim construction, types of infringement, defenses (including invalidity and prior art), and statutory theories (e.g., §271 variants and means-plus-function). Intended to guide jury findings and trial judge's charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent claims are numbered sentences at the end of the patent and are intended to define, in words, the boundaries of the inventor’s rights. Only the claims of the patent can be infringed; neither the written description nor the drawings can be infringed. Each claim must be considered individually. You must use the same claim meaning for both your decision on infringement and your decision on invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must understand claims before deciding infringement or invalidity; judge supplies claim meanings. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Phillips v. AWH; Markman; Catalina Lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for the Case (judge-provided constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge provides the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted and the jury must accept those meanings when deciding infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]. Judge's constructions control. (Cites Teva Pharm. v. Sandoz; Phillips; Markman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function (§112(f)/¶6) Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim uses a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, that clause may be a means-plus-function element requiring special interpretation; it does not cover all means/steps that perform the recited function. The court identifies the recited function and the structure (or step) in the specification/drawings that performs it, or equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must use the court's interpretation of the means-plus-function element for infringement and validity. Consider whether Instruction 2.2 is necessary where the phrase 'means for' is not used but §112(f) may apply. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 112; Mettler-Toledo; JVW; Utah Med.; Valmont.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner has the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the U.S. during the term of the patent. Any person or entity engaging in those acts without permission infringes the patent. A claim may be infringed directly or indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding infringement, compare the accused product/method to the patent claims (not to the plaintiff’s commercial product). Distinguish direct vs indirect infringement, literal infringement vs doctrine of equivalents, and induced vs contributory infringement. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271; Limelight; WordTech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge and Intent Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant is liable for direct infringement if the plaintiff proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim. The defendant can directly infringe without knowing of the patent or knowing that their actions are infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement is a strict-liability rule as to knowledge/intent. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Commil; Medtronic v. Mirowski; Global-Tech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement (all-elements rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element or method step recited in that patent claim. If the accused product/method lacks one or more elements, it does not literally infringe that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement with respect to each claim individually. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element. Use the court's claim constructions when comparing. (Cites Limelight; Hutchins; Amstar.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement (attribution rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple parties perform steps of a claimed method, the defendant is liable only if the defendant personally performed all acts necessary to infringe or if the acts of others are attributable to the defendant via direction or control or formation of a joint enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: (1) agreement among group members; (2) common purpose to be carried out by group; (3) community of pecuniary interest in that purpose; and (4) equal right to a voice in the direction of the enterprise. If neither direction/control nor joint enterprise is found, no direct infringement. (Cites Limelight; Akamai; Eli Lilly; Nalco.) Practice note: Explain joint infringement and inducement side-by-side to avoid jury confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function or Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement of a means-plus-function/step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove (1) the accused product/method performs the recited function and (2) the accused structure/step is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the patent specification and drawings for performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First decide whether the accused product has any structure/step that performs the specific function. If so, decide whether that structure/step is the same as, or equivalent to, the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence is judged from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art—differences are insubstantial if they perform the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. (Cites §112; Williamson; Brilliant Instruments; Cybor; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims do not refer to other claims. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements recited in the dependent claim as well as all elements of the independent claim to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, the plaintiff must show the accused product/method includes each and every element of the independent claim and the dependent claim. If the independent claim is not literally infringed, the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed. (Cites Wahpeton Canvas; Shatterproof Glass.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Comprising', 'Consisting of', and 'Consisting Essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' means including the following but not excluding others. 'Consisting of' means including the following and excluding others. 'Consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly including unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim uses 'comprising', the presence of additional components/steps does not defeat literal infringement. If 'consisting of' is used, additional components/steps defeat literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of' is used, additional components/steps are permitted only if they do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. Practice note: If claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to the doctrine of equivalents. (Cites cases including Shire Dev.; Multilayer; PPG.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents—When Literal Infringement Fails
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if it contains components/steps that are equivalents of the claim elements that are not literally present. The accused product must have an equivalent for each individual claim element that is not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence may be shown by demonstrating the accused component performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result, or by showing it is insubstantially different. Consider whether persons of ordinary skill would have known of interchangeability at the time, though known interchangeability is not necessary. The same accused component may satisfy multiple claim elements; multiple accused components may satisfy a single claim element. (Cites Warner-Jenkinson; Graver Tank.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents Limitation—Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee made a representation or argument, or an amendment to the claim for reasons related to patentability, there is a presumption that the equivalent subject matter has been surrendered and the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements unless the presumption is rebutted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is determined by the court as a matter of law. If applied, the judge will list elements on a claim-by-claim basis to which DOE cannot be applied; those elements must be literally present for infringement. (Cites Festo; Federal Circuit authority.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents Limitation—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court determines certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements; they must be literally present for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will list affected elements on a claim-by-claim basis. (Cites SanDisk; Pfizer v. Teva; Johnson & Johnston.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement) — Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that the defendant actively induced infringement, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps) and (2) the defendant actively induced these acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove inducement the plaintiff must establish that (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts constituting direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires subjective belief of a high probability a patent existed plus deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. (Cites §271(b); Commil; Limelight; Global-Tech.) Practice note: Distinguish inducement from joint infringement in jury instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supplying All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantial portion of components requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment; exporting a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). (Cites §271(f)(1); Life Techs. v. Promega; Microsoft v. AT&T.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement—Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To find contributory infringement, the plaintiff must prove someone other than the defendant directly infringed a claim and that the defendant (1) sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (2) the component/apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (3) the component/apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (4) the defendant knew the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' has other non-infringing uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (subjective high probability plus deliberate avoidance). (Cites §271(c); Commil; Global-Tech; Aro; Toshiba.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supplying Components Especially Made/Adapted for Use Abroad (§271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant supplied components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) the defendant knew or should have known the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product—intended combination suffices. (Cites §271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft; Cardiac Pacemakers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Import/Sale/Offer for Sale/Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts defendant infringed by importing, selling, offering for sale, or using a product that was made by a process covered by one or more patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show infringement under §271(g) plaintiff must prove: (1) defendant imported/sold/offered/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim; (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and expiration (or trial); and (3) defendant acted between those dates. If the product was materially changed by later processes or is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product, it was not 'made by' the claimed process. (Cites §271(g); Amgen v. Roche; NTP v. RIM.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense—Burden and Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends asserted claims are invalid and must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will instruct jury in more detail about defendant's specific invalidity contentions. (Standard: clear and convincing evidence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes any product or method publicly known or used by others in the U.S. before the claimed invention was invented; any product/method in public use or on sale in the U.S. before the cutoff date; patents that issued before the cutoff date; publications having dates of public accessibility before the cutoff date; and any product/method made by anyone in the U.S. before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a given case the court will identify the prior art admitted into evidence. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA).)
